Chapter Four: The Wreck Survey

The survey team returned to the site at first light, when the water was flat and the buoys sat motionless above the sand. Their chart showed a broad ridge running north to south, cut by a channel that had shifted several metres since the previous season. On the earlier visit the team had spent three days mapping the outer hull, and those drawings were still pinned to the cabin wall beneath a brass ruler. A second set, drawn in pencil on tracing paper, lay rolled inside a cardboard tube beside the door. Nobody had expected the site to be so well preserved.

Diving in pairs, they worked short shifts and logged every artefact in a waterproof notebook. A brass compass, a clay pipe, and a scatter of bottle glass came up first. Later came a copper spike and a length of rope that had hardened into a dark crust. Each item was bagged, numbered, and photographed against a grey scale before being lifted to the boat. The notebook filled quickly, and the second diver kept a running list on a slate in grease pencil. Above them the boat rolled gently, and the engine ticked as it cooled.

By noon the wind had freshened and the swell pushed through the channel, so the diving slowed. The supervisor, a quiet woman named Marit Solheim, called a halt and sent the team back to the surface. Over sandwiches in the wheelhouse she went through the plan for the afternoon: a narrow trench along the port side, then a full photographic record of the exposed frames before the tide turned. The forecast promised rain by evening, which would muddy the water and cost them a day.

After lunch they concentrated on the main cargo area, where the sand was finest and the visibility best. The ballast stones had settled into a single dense layer, and beneath it the timber frames were still joined by oak pegs. It was here, at the bottom of the hold, that they found the lead weights stamped with the maker's mark. Solheim photographed the find where it lay, then lifted the largest weight by hand and passed it up to the waiting diver.

The conservation laboratory in the old customs house took the material the following week. Every object was soaked in fresh water, brushed, and dried on racks under a slow fan. The team argued about the label on one crate for a whole morning, and in the end they simply wrote unidentified on the side and moved on to the next box. Funding for the next season was still uncertain, but nobody in the crew seemed to doubt that they would be back on the water by spring.
